title: The Queen Who Would Not Come
subtitle: Esther 1:1–22
description: Xerxes feasts for 180 days, and Queen Vashti refuses to come. A decree no one can repeal empties the throne.
paragraphs: The empire ran from India to the far south, and one man reigned over all of it. The book opens with his name and his reach: “This is what happened in the days of Xerxes, who reigned over 127 provinces from India to Cush.” In the third year of his reign, seated on his throne in the citadel of Susa, the king put the whole empire on display in a single long celebration, and the celebration is where this story starts, because everything in Esther seems to happen at a table. One more thing about this book belongs at the front, stated once and plainly: in all ten chapters, God is never named. No prophet speaks, no prayer is recorded, and the telling that follows will not add what the book leaves out.

The feast ran in two parts. First came the display: "And for a full 180 days he displayed the glorious riches of his kingdom and the magnificent splendor of his greatness," with the military leaders of Persia and Media, the nobles, and the princes of the provinces all assembled to see it. Then, in the garden court of the palace, the king held a seven-day feast for everyone in the citadel, from the least to the greatest, under hangings of white and blue linen on marble pillars, on couches of gold and silver. “Beverages were served in an array of goblets of gold, each with a different design, and the royal wine flowed freely, according to the king’s bounty.” By the king's own order, “no limit was placed on the drinking.” Across the palace, Queen Vashti gave a banquet of her own for the women.

On the seventh day, with the king's heart merry with wine, he sent his seven eunuchs to fetch the queen, wearing her royal crown, “to display her beauty to the people and officials. For she was beautiful to behold.” The answer came back through the same eunuchs, and it was no. “Queen Vashti, however, refused to come at the king’s command brought by his eunuchs. And the king became furious, and his anger burned within him.” The book gives no reason for her refusal. It does not quote her, defend her, or condemn her. A queen who would not come, a king burning in front of his court, and a question of law where a marriage question should have been: that is all the text provides, and it is enough to move an empire.

The king consulted his wise men, the experts in law and justice who had personal access to him, and put the matter formally: “what should be done with Queen Vashti, since she refused to obey the command of King Xerxes delivered by the eunuchs?” Memucan, one of the seven princes, answered, and he widened the offense until it filled the map. “Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king, but all the princes and the peoples in all the provinces of King Xerxes.” Every wife in 127 provinces would hear of it and despise her husband, he argued, and the noble women of Persia and Media would start that very day. His remedy matched his alarm: let the king “issue a royal decree, and let it be recorded in the laws of Persia and Media so that it cannot be repealed, that Vashti shall never again enter the presence of King Xerxes.” A law that cannot be repealed, made to settle a household quarrel. Remember the mechanism. This book will need it again.

The counsel pleased the king and his princes, and it was done as Memucan advised. Letters went out to every province in its own script and every people in its own language, “proclaiming that every man should be master of his own household.” That is how Esther begins: a feast that lasted half a year, a crown carried back unused, and an empire-wide decree about husbands and wives, issued because one woman would not cross a courtyard. The throne now had a vacancy the law itself had carved, and somewhere out in the city of Susa, unmentioned so far, lived an exiled Jewish family with a daughter whose name the court had never heard.

title: Esther Crowned, and a Deed in the Record
subtitle: Esther 2:1–23
description: An exiled orphan is crowned queen, and her cousin's deed at the gate is written into a book nobody reads. Yet.
paragraphs: Some time later the king's anger cooled, and he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what had been decreed against her. The decree could not be repealed, so the throne's vacancy had to be filled another way. His attendants proposed a search across the empire: “Let a search be made for beautiful young virgins for the king.” Commissioners in every province would assemble the women into the harem at Susa under Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the women, and the young woman who pleased the king would become queen in place of Vashti. The suggestion pleased the king, and he acted on it. The empire that had legislated about wives now went looking for one.

It is here, in a palace search, that the book finally introduces its own people. “Now there was at the citadel of Susa a Jewish man from the tribe of Benjamin named Mordecai son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish.” His family had come east in the exile generations before: “He had been carried into exile from Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon among those taken captive with Jeconiah king of Judah.” And Mordecai had raised a cousin who had no one else. “And Mordecai had brought up Hadassah (that is, Esther), the daughter of his uncle, because she did not have a father or mother.” When her parents died, “Mordecai had taken her as his own daughter.” She was lovely in form and appearance, the text says, and when the king's command was proclaimed and many young women were gathered at Susa, Esther was taken too, to the palace, under Hegai's care.

Inside the harem she found favor quickly. “And the young woman pleased him and obtained his favor, so he quickly provided her with beauty treatments and the special diet.” Hegai assigned her seven select maidservants from the palace and moved her to the best place in the harem. But one thing she did not do, on Mordecai's standing instruction: “Esther did not reveal her people or her lineage, because Mordecai had instructed her not to do so.” The book gives no reason for the silence beyond the instruction itself. And every day, outside, Mordecai walked back and forth in front of the court of the harem, to learn how she was and what was happening to her.

The process ran a full year for every woman in the harem, six months with oil of myrrh and six with perfumes and cosmetics, and then her single evening with the king, after which she would not return unless he delighted in her and summoned her by name. When Esther's turn came, she went differently from the rest: “she did not ask for anything except what Hegai, the king’s trusted official in charge of the harem, had advised. And Esther found favor in the eyes of everyone who saw her.” She was taken to the king in the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign, four years after Vashti's refusal. “And the king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she found grace and favor in his sight more than all of the other virgins.” He placed the royal crown on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti, then held a great banquet in her name, proclaimed a tax holiday in the provinces, and gave gifts worthy of his bounty. An exiled orphan sat on the throne of Persia, and no one in the palace knew whose daughter she was.

The episode ends at the king's gate, and the ending matters more than the crown. The virgins were assembled a second time, and Mordecai was sitting at the gate in some official place, and Esther still kept her secret: “Esther still had not revealed her lineage or her people, just as Mordecai had instructed. She obeyed Mordecai’s command, as she had done under his care.” In those days two of the king's eunuchs, Bigthan and Teresh, who guarded the entrance, grew angry and conspired to assassinate Xerxes. Mordecai learned of the plot and reported it to Queen Esther, and she informed the king on Mordecai's behalf. The report was investigated and verified, both men were hanged, and the account was written down: “And all this was recorded in the Book of the Chronicles in the presence of the king.” A deed done, a name recorded, a book closed on a shelf in the palace. Nothing came of it. Not yet.

title: Haman's Lot
subtitle: Esther 3:1–15
description: Haman rises, Mordecai will not bow, and the lot picks a day for a people's destruction.
paragraphs: After these events, the king elevated a new chief over all his princes: Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite. The king commanded every royal servant at the gate to bow down and pay him homage, and they did, all of them, except one. “But Mordecai would not bow down or pay homage.” The servants at the gate pressed him on it day after day. Why do you disobey the command of the king? He would not comply, and in the end he told them the one fact he had kept even from the palace about his own household: he had told them he was a Jew. They reported the matter to Haman, to see whether Mordecai's behavior would be tolerated. The book never states Mordecai's reason for refusing. It states the refusal, the fact he gave, and nothing more.

When Haman saw for himself that Mordecai would not bow, “he was filled with rage.” Then he learned whose people Mordecai belonged to, and the rage changed its shape. “And when he learned the identity of Mordecai’s people, he scorned the notion of laying hands on Mordecai alone. Instead, he sought to destroy all of Mordecai’s people, the Jews, throughout the kingdom of Xerxes.” One man's stiff neck became, in Haman's accounting, a sentence on every Jew in 127 provinces. Before he moved, he consulted the lot. “In the twelfth year of King Xerxes, in the first month, the month of Nisan, the Pur (that is, the lot) was cast before Haman to determine a day and month. And the lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar.” The date of a people's destruction was chosen by dice, nearly a year away.

Then Haman went to the king, and his pitch never named his real quarrel. “There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples of every province of your kingdom. Their laws are different from everyone else’s, and they do not obey the king’s laws. So it is not in the king’s best interest to tolerate them.” A certain people, scattered, different, disobedient. He did not say which people, and the king did not ask. Haman offered to sweeten the proposal himself: “If it pleases the king, let a decree be issued to destroy them, and I will deposit ten thousand talents of silver into the royal treasury to pay those who carry it out.”

The king took off his signet ring and gave it to his new chief, and the text names Haman in full for the first time at the moment of the gift: “So the king removed the signet ring from his finger and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.” The money he waved away. “These people are given to you to do with them as you please.” On the thirteenth day of Nisan the royal scribes were summoned, and the order was written exactly as Haman commanded, to the satraps, the governors, and the officials of every people, in the script of each province and the language of every people, written in the king's name and sealed with the king's ring. The letters ordered the provinces “to destroy, kill, and annihilate all the Jews,” young and old, women and children, “and to plunder their possessions on a single day, the thirteenth day of Adar, the twelfth month.” Read that sealing again, because the mechanism matters: a decree written in the king's name and sealed with his ring cannot be repealed, not even by the king. Haman had built the trap out of the empire's own law.

The couriers rode out, spurred on by the king's command, and the edict was published in every province so the people would be ready on that day. In the citadel, the two men who had set it in motion marked the occasion in the manner this book knows best. “Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion.” A feast at the top, bewilderment in the streets below, and eleven months of waiting now stood between the Jews of the empire and the day the lot had chosen.

title: If I Perish, I Perish
subtitle: Esther 4:1–17
description: Sackcloth at the gate, messages through a eunuch, and a queen decides: if I perish, I perish.
paragraphs: Mordecai heard what had been decreed, and the whole city could hear his answer. “When Mordecai learned of all that had happened, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, wailing loudly and bitterly.” He went only as far as the king's gate, because the law barred anyone in sackcloth from entering it. Nor was he alone in the mourning. Everywhere the edict arrived, the same scene repeated: “In every province to which the king’s command and edict came, there was great mourning among the Jews. They fasted, wept, and lamented, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.” In the palace, behind the walls, the queen heard about a man in ashes at the gate before she heard why he was wearing them.

Esther's maidens and eunuchs told her of Mordecai, and she was overcome with distress. Her first response was to fix the visible problem: she sent clothes for him to wear instead of his sackcloth, and he refused them. So she sent Hathach, a eunuch appointed to her, to learn what was troubling him and why. Mordecai told him everything, including the exact amount of money Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury, and he handed over a copy of the written decree itself, the cold text of it, “urging her to approach the king, implore his favor, and plead before him for her people.” The hidden queen now held her people's death warrant in her own hands, in a document that did not know her name.

Her reply was not fear talking; it was the law, stated precisely. Everyone in the empire knew it: “one law applies to every man or woman who approaches the king in the inner court without being summoned.” The sentence was death. “Only if the king extends the gold scepter may that person live.” And the last fact was personal: “But I have not been summoned to appear before the king for the past thirty days.” Thirty days of silence from the throne. A queen who had found favor once, four years and one new favorite minister ago, being asked to walk uninvited into the inner court and stake her life on a scepter. Mordecai's answer came back through the same messenger, and it is the sharpest speech in the book.

“Do not imagine that because you are in the king’s palace you alone will escape the fate of all the Jews.” The palace walls would not hold back an empire-wide edict, and a hidden name cannot stay hidden forever. Then came the line the whole book turns on, spoken by a man in sackcloth who names no rescuer: “For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” Deliverance would arise, from another place, if she stayed silent. That is as close as this book ever comes to saying out loud where help comes from, and Mordecai leaves the phrase exactly there, unclaimed and unadorned, with a question attached: who knows if this is why you are where you are?

Esther's reply reversed the direction of command. The cousin who had raised her and instructed her all her life now received instructions from the queen. “Go and assemble all the Jews who can be found in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day, and I and my maidens will fast as you do. After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!” No meal opens this book's crisis; a fast does, three days of an entire community not eating, inside a story that has done nothing but feast. “So Mordecai went and did all that Esther had instructed him.” The gate and the palace had traded places. Now the three days had to run.

title: The First Banquet and the Gallows
subtitle: Esther 5:1–14
description: The scepter is extended, the request is deferred, and a gallows fifty cubits high goes up in the night.
paragraphs: On the third day of the fast, Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the palace, across from the king's quarters, where he sat on his throne facing the entrance. She had not been summoned. The law she had quoted to Hathach now stood between her and the man on the throne, and the whole story paused on what his hand would do. “As soon as the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she found favor in his sight. The king extended the gold scepter in his hand toward Esther, and she approached and touched the tip of the scepter.” She would live. The king spoke first, and generously: “What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be given to you.”

Her request, after three days of fasting and a walk that could have killed her, was dinner. “If it pleases the king,” Esther replied, “may the king and Haman come today to the banquet I have prepared for the king.” No accusation, no plea, no name named. The king commanded Haman to be brought in a hurry, and the two most powerful men in the empire came to the queen's table. As they drank their wine, the king asked again: “What is your petition? It will be given to you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be fulfilled.” This was the moment, and Esther let it pass. “If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and fulfill my request, may the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet I will prepare for them. Then I will answer the king’s question.” The text offers no reason why she waited. It records the delay and moves on, and the delay turns out to be the hinge of everything, because of what happened that night.

Haman left the banquet glowing. The queen had invited no one but him to sit with the king, and she had invited him back. At the king's gate, though, stood the one flaw in his day. He saw Mordecai, “who did not rise or tremble in fear at his presence. And Haman was filled with rage toward Mordecai.” He restrained himself, went home, and called for his wife Zeresh and his friends to hear the inventory of his greatness: his wealth, his many sons, every way the king had honored and promoted him above the other officials.

The inventory ended in a confession. “Queen Esther invited no one but me to join the king at the banquet she prepared, and I am invited back tomorrow along with the king.” Then: “Yet none of this satisfies me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.” All the wealth, all the sons, all the honor in the empire, and one unbending man at a gate outweighed the lot of it. His wife and his friends had a remedy sized to the obsession: “Have them build a gallows fifty cubits high, and ask the king in the morning to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go to the banquet with the king and enjoy yourself.” Fifty cubits, roughly seventy-five feet of timber, a gallows tall enough to be seen across the city, built for an execution the king had not yet been asked to approve. The advice pleased Haman, and he had it built that night.

So the night before the second banquet held two new facts that had not existed at sundown: a gallows standing ready at Haman's house, and a queen's unanswered petition waiting for tomorrow. What the night would do with the man who had built the gallows, and with the king who had to be asked to use it, belongs to the next episode. It begins with a king who could not sleep.

title: The King Could Not Sleep
subtitle: Esther 6:1–14
description: The king cannot sleep, the chronicles are read, and Haman parades the man he came to hang.
paragraphs: The text says it plainly and says no more about why: “That night sleep escaped the king.” A king who could summon anything in 127 provinces could not summon sleep, so he ordered the empire's record brought instead: “so he ordered the Book of Records, the Chronicles, to be brought in and read to him.” Of all the scrolls in the palace, the reader's place fell on an entry five years old, and the entry was a name the king had never properly heard. “And there it was found recorded that Mordecai had exposed Bigthana and Teresh, two of the eunuchs who guarded the king’s entrance, when they had conspired to assassinate King Xerxes.” The deed Esther had reported in Mordecai's name, investigated, punished, written down, and forgotten, read aloud in the dark to the man it had saved.

The king asked the obvious question. “What honor or dignity has been bestowed on Mordecai for this act?” The attendants' answer was the truth of the whole reign in four words: “Nothing has been done for him.” Then the king asked who was in the court, and the timing is the story's own, offered without comment: Haman had just entered the outer court, at dawn, come early to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he had prepared. Before Haman could speak his errand, the king put his question to the one man in the empire who would answer it as a description of himself. “What should be done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor?” And Haman thought what the text lets us hear: “Whom would the king be delighted to honor more than me?”

So Haman designed the honor he was sure was coming to him, and he designed it royally. “For the man whom the king is delighted to honor, have them bring a royal robe that the king himself has worn and a horse on which the king himself has ridden.” Not new clothes, the king's own clothes. Not any horse, the king's own horse, with a royal crest on its head. The robe and horse were to be handed to one of the king's most noble princes, who would array the man and parade him through the city square, proclaiming before him: “This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!” Every element of it, the robe, the horse, the herald prince, the public square, came out of Haman's imagination in one speech, because no one in that court knew better than Haman what supreme honor looked like. He had been picturing it for years.

The king's answer named the honoree. “Hurry,” said the king to Haman, “and do just as you proposed. Take the robe and the horse to Mordecai the Jew, who is sitting at the king’s gate. Do not neglect anything that you have suggested.” Do not neglect anything. Haman took the robe and the horse, arrayed the man he had come to hang, and led him through the square of Susa crying the proclamation before him with his own voice, the most noble prince in the empire serving as herald to the Jew at the gate. When it was done, “Mordecai returned to the king’s gate,” back to his post, in his own clothes, as if nothing had happened.

Haman rushed home with his head covered in grief and told Zeresh and his friends everything. The household that had advised the gallows now read the morning differently: “Since Mordecai, before whom your downfall has begun, is Jewish, you will not prevail against him.” And the sentence finishes on the far side of the text's own dash: “for surely you will fall before him.” Downfall has begun, his own wife said. While they were still speaking, the king's eunuchs arrived at the door and rushed Haman to the banquet Esther had prepared, ready or not.

title: This Wicked Man
subtitle: Esther 7:1–10
description: At the second banquet the queen names the enemy, and the gallows finds its man.
paragraphs: The king and Haman came to dine with Esther a second time, Haman rushed from the conversation in which his own wife had called this morning the beginning of his downfall. As they drank their wine, the king asked once more, the promise now made three times in two days: “Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given to you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be fulfilled.” The deferral was over. Whatever Esther had been doing with that extra day, the account she had come through the law to give was now due, and everyone at the table knew the king had asked too many times to be refused again.

She began as a petitioner, in the court's own language of favor, and then she asked for the one thing no one had expected a queen to need. “If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it pleases the king, grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request.” My life. My people. The hidden name of four years came out of hiding in a single sentence, and the reason followed immediately: “For my people and I have been sold out to destruction, death, and annihilation.” Sold, she said, past tense, a transaction already sealed with the king's own ring, which the king himself had handed over in this story's third act without asking what it would buy. And she measured her silence, too: “If we had merely been sold as menservants and maidservants, I would have remained silent.” Slavery she would have borne quietly. Annihilation she would not.

The king spoke up then, and his question shows he truly had never known what he had signed. “Who is this, and where is the one who would devise such a scheme?” Only one man at the table knew, and the queen named him in a sentence the text itself breaks with a dash, as if the pointing had to happen before the name could land: “The adversary and enemy is this wicked man,” she said. Haman. “And Haman stood in terror before the king and queen.” Every thread of the man's two days ran through this room: the ring he had been given, the edict he had written, the gallows he had built, the parade he had led that morning, and now the queen he had twice dined with, turning out to be one of the people his letters had condemned.

In his fury the king rose from the wine and went out to the palace garden. Haman stayed behind to beg the queen for his life, for he understood the king was planning a terrible fate for him. At exactly the wrong moment the king returned from the garden, just as Haman, pleading, was falling across the couch where Esther reclined. The scene read itself to a suspicious king in the worst possible way. “Would he actually assault the queen while I am in the palace?” As soon as the words left the king's mouth, they covered Haman's face, the gesture that meant the sentence had already been passed. No trial was coming. The covering of the face was the trial.

What remained was the instrument, and a servant supplied it, with the two facts that sealed the matter joined in one sentence. Harbonah, one of the eunuchs attending the king, spoke up: “There is a gallows fifty cubits high at Haman’s house. He had it built for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king.” The gallows built overnight for the king's rescuer, mentioned within earshot of the king at the hour of Haman's fall. “Hang him on it!” declared the king. “So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the fury of the king subsided.” But notice what the hanging did not do. It did not touch the letters. Thirteen days into Adar was still coming on every Jew in the empire, sealed with a ring that no law of Persia and Media could unseal, and killing the author had not killed the edict.

title: Light and Gladness
subtitle: Esther 8:1–17
description: Haman's ring changes hands, a second decree answers the first, and Susa shouts.
paragraphs: That same day the king gave Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews, everything the fallen chief had owned. And Mordecai entered the king's presence, because Esther had revealed his relation to her; the man who had sat at the gate in sackcloth was now inside, and known. The symbols of Haman's rise all changed hands in a single verse. “The king removed the signet ring he had recovered from Haman and presented it to Mordecai. And Esther appointed Mordecai over the estate of Haman.” The ring that had sealed the edict against the Jews now sat on the finger of the Jew it was meant to erase. It was a complete reversal of position. It was not yet a rescue, because the edict still stood, and Mordecai of all people knew Persian law.

So Esther went to the king again, and this time there was no robe, no banquet, and no deferral. She fell at his feet weeping, “and begged him to revoke the evil scheme of Haman the Agagite, which he had devised against the Jews.” The king extended the gold scepter toward her, and she rose and stood, and her request was a piece of legal writing, aimed at the letters themselves: “may an order be written to revoke the letters that the scheming Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king’s provinces.” Then the lawyer's voice gave way to the cousin's. “For how could I bear to see the disaster that would befall my people? How could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?” Twice in two days the queen had risked the inner court. The first time she came for an audience. This time she came back because winning the audience had not been enough.

The king's answer named the problem exactly, and in naming it, opened the only door Persian law had left. He had given Haman's estate to Esther, and Haman had been hanged because he attacked the Jews. But the first edict could not simply be withdrawn, and the king said so in the book's own legal formula: “Now you may write in the king’s name as you please regarding the Jews, and seal it with the royal signet ring. For a decree that is written in the name of the king and sealed with the royal signet ring cannot be revoked.” What could not be revoked could be answered. A second decree, written by the intended victims, sealed with the same ring, riding to the same provinces, to stand alongside the first on the appointed day. Memucan's mechanism, the unchangeable law, had shut the Jews in. The same mechanism would now have to carry them out.

At once the scribes were summoned, on the twenty-third day of Sivan, two months and more after Haman's letters, and they recorded all of Mordecai's orders, to the Jews and to the satraps, governors, and princes of the 127 provinces, each province in its own script, each people in its own language, and the Jews in theirs. “Mordecai wrote in the name of King Xerxes and sealed it with the royal signet ring. He sent the documents by mounted couriers riding on swift horses bred from the royal mares.” The permission the letters carried was the mirror image of the first decree's: “By these letters the king permitted the Jews in each and every city the right to assemble and defend themselves.” Where Haman's edict had armed a day against them, Mordecai's armed them for it. And the day appointed was the same day, the thirteenth of Adar, the day the lot had chosen before either decree existed.

Then the man who had wailed in sackcloth in the middle of the city walked out of the palace dressed like the parade he had been led through. Mordecai went out from the king's presence in royal garments of blue and white, with a large gold crown and a purple robe of fine linen. “And the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.” The city that had been in confusion at the first edict shouted at the second. “For the Jews it was a time of light and gladness, of joy and honor.” In every province the king's decree reached, there was feasting and celebrating among the Jews, and the book records one further effect without explaining it: “And many of the people of the land themselves became Jews, because the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.” The letters had done their work. Now the thirteenth of Adar had to arrive, and both decrees would meet on the same day.

title: Purim: The Days That Were Turned
subtitle: Esther 9:1–10:3
description: The day is overturned, the plunder is refused three times, and Purim enters the calendar forever.
paragraphs: The thirteenth of Adar arrived, the day the lot had picked out a year before either edict existed, and both of the king's decrees stood in force over it at once. The chapter opens by naming what happened with the book's own word for the whole story: “On this day the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, but their plan was overturned and the Jews overpowered those who hated them.” In city after city the Jews assembled to attack those who sought to harm them, and no man could withstand them, because fear of them had fallen on all peoples. The officials of the empire, the satraps, the governors, and the king's administrators, helped the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them. The man whose name had once been reported to the king by an informer was now a power in the palace whose fame ran ahead of the fighting.

In the citadel of Susa the Jews killed five hundred men, and among them, named one by one in the record, all ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. The account of the day then makes a point it will make twice more before the chapter ends, a point about what the Jews did not do with their victory: “They killed these ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” Both edicts had permitted plunder. The record is careful, three separate times, to say the permission was never used.

That day's count from the citadel was reported to the king, and the king brought it to Esther himself, with the offer still open: five hundred dead in Susa, including Haman's ten sons, and what more did she request? Her request is the hardest verse in the book to read slowly, and it is told here exactly as the text tells it. “If it pleases the king, may the Jews in Susa also have tomorrow to carry out today’s edict, and may the bodies of Haman’s ten sons be hanged on the gallows.” The king commanded that it be done. On the fourteenth the Jews of Susa assembled again and put to death three hundred men there, and the record repeats its refrain: “but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” In the provinces the rest of the Jews assembled to defend themselves and killed 75,000 who hated them, “but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” Three times the same sentence, standing over three fields of the same war, and then the fighting stopped, and the rest began: the provinces on the fourteenth day, Susa on the fifteenth, each resting the day after its own fighting, and making the rest day a day of feasting and joy.

Mordecai wrote it all down and sent letters to every Jew in the empire, near and far, to bind the days into the calendar forever: the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar, kept every year, “as the days on which the Jews gained rest from their enemies and the month in which their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday.” The days were to be marked by feasting and joy, by sending gifts to one another, and by gifts to the poor. The name came from the weapon Haman had used to choose his day: he had cast the Pur, the lot, to crush and destroy them, and so “these days are called Purim, from the word Pur.” The dice that picked the date of their destruction were turned into the name of their feast, which is the whole book in one sentence. The Jews bound themselves and their descendants and all who would join them never to let the days fail, and Esther added her own authority to Mordecai's: “So Queen Esther daughter of Abihail, along with Mordecai the Jew, wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter concerning Purim.” Mordecai's letters went out to all the Jews in the 127 provinces, and their contents are worth ending on: they were letters carrying “words of peace and truth.”

The book then closes with three short verses that belong to Mordecai alone. The king imposed his tribute to the farthest shores, as kings do, and the record of Mordecai's greatness stands written where such records stand, in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia. The last word on the man who began the story sitting unnoticed at a gate is this: “For Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Xerxes, preeminent among the Jews and highly favored by his many kinsmen, seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his countrymen.” Esther's book ends there, on peace spoken to a whole people by the cousin who once paced outside a harem wall. The return story resumes where the series left it: in Jerusalem, with Nehemiah, and a wall.
